User is interested in the history of the #Olympics, especially how the Games have reflected geopolitical tensions and been used as a political tool. #geopolitics

The ancient #Olympics began in 776 B.C. at Olympia, Greece, held every four years in honor of Zeus (running, jumping, throwing). The modern Games were revived in 1896 in Athens with 14 nations competing in 43 events. #history
The 1936 Berlin #Olympics were held under Nazi rule and used as propaganda to showcase Nazi ideology and Aryan supremacy, sparking controversy and some boycotts. #geopolitics
During the Cold War the #Olympics became a US vs. Soviet Union battleground, with fierce rivalry in gymnastics, track and field, and basketball. #geopolitics
At the 1972 Munich #Olympics, 11 Israeli athletes were killed by Palestinian terrorists, heightening tensions and security at later Games. #geopolitics
The 1980 Moscow #Olympics were boycotted by several Western nations, led by the US, in protest of the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan. #geopolitics #boycott

At the 1968 Mexico City #Olympics, US sprinters Tommie Smith and John Carlos raised their fists on the podium during the anthem to protest racial discrimination — an iconic moment in the civil rights movement. #athlete_protest

At the 2000 Sydney #Olympics, Aboriginal sprinter Cathy Freeman carried both the Australian and Aboriginal flags on her victory lap after winning the 400m, a gesture of reconciliation with Indigenous Australians. #athlete_protest
The 2018 Pyeongchang Winter #Olympics saw North and South Korean teams march together, seen as a sign of political reconciliation, though some viewed it as North Korean propaganda. #geopolitics

The 2022 Beijing Winter #Olympics faced controversy over human rights abuses in Xinjiang and China's treatment of Hong Kong and Taiwan, with some countries calling for a boycott. #geopolitics #boycott
The 2020 Tokyo #Olympics were postponed by the COVID-19 pandemic and held without spectators; critics said the event was prioritized over public health. #geopolitics

User is interested in the British Grand Fleet in World War I: its tactics, intelligence operations, ship types, and internal resistance to reform. #GrandFleet #WWI

Admiral John "Jackie" Fisher proposed the battlecruiser concept in the early 1900s: faster than battleships but lightly armored, intended for scouting, raiding, and trade protection. Many Royal Navy officers were skeptical of the lighter armor. #GrandFleet #WWI #battlecruisers

Within the Royal Navy, conservative senior officers resisted new tactics (battlecruisers, destroyer screens) because they trained in the late 19th-century battleship-centric era, feared the cost and risk of unproven methods, and distrusted ideas that challenged established doctrine. #GrandFleet #WWI #naval-doctrine

Room 40 was the Admiralty's secret signals-intelligence unit in WWI, intercepting and decoding German communications; its intelligence supported the blockade of Germany, U-boat avoidance, and the Battle of Jutland in 1916. #GrandFleet #WWI #Room40 #signals-intelligence

Covert/notable Grand Fleet-related operations discussed: the naval blockade of Germany; 1918 Baltic Sea minelaying operation against the German Navy; the 1918 Zeebrugge Raid (blocking the harbor with blockships, ~200 British servicemen killed). #GrandFleet #WWI #Zeebrugge

Ship types of the Grand Fleet and their roles: battleships (main battle line, flagships), battlecruisers (scouting, baiting enemy), cruisers (scouting, convoy escort), destroyers (torpedo screening of capital ships), plus seaplanes for reconnaissance. #GrandFleet #WWI

User believes outdated strategies cannot win wars and pressed on why officers resisted new tactics; they responded well to explanations of institutional conservatism, cost/risk aversion, and coordination difficulties. #GrandFleet #user-views

Correction worth remembering: some earlier Grand Fleet answers contained errors — the Grand Fleet was overwhelmingly British (not a multinational fleet with language barriers), submarines were not part of its battle fleet, and Jutland (1916) is generally judged a tactical draw or German tactical success, not a British tactical victory. #GrandFleet #WWI #corrections
